tasks.entryDescription: Radon's theorem plus induction; minimal subfamily and affine dependence; nerve/topological methods for generalizations.
tasks.currentSketch: Assume every d+1 of a finite family of convex sets intersect. Induct on family size; apply Radon’s theorem to points x_i chosen from intersections omitting C_i. A Radon partition yields a point lying in every C_i, contradiction otherwise. The finite-family theorem follows; topological nerve versions require additional hypotheses such as contractibility.

tasks.entryName: Radon's theorem for finite point sets
tasks.entryDescription: Affine dependence and sign partition; convex-hull separation; linear-algebra nullspace argument.
tasks.currentSketch: For d+2 points x_i∈R^d, find a nonzero affine dependence Σa_ix_i=0 and Σa_i=0. Positive and negative coefficients both occur; normalize their absolute sums to 1. The two convex combinations then agree, so the convex hulls of the positive- and negative-coefficient point sets intersect.

existingReferences.label: Matoušek, Lectures on Discrete Geometry
existingReferences.locator: Chapter 1, Radon theorem

tasks.entryName: Radon's theorem for finite point sets
tasks.entryDescription: Affine dependence and sign partition; convex-hull separation; linear-algebra nullspace argument.
tasks.currentSketch: Suppose, for contradiction, every partition of d+2 points into two parts has disjoint convex hulls. Strict separation then supplies a hyperplane separating each pair of hulls. The sign patterns of these separating affine functionals cannot realize all required dichotomies of d+2 points in R^d (affine halfspaces have VC dimension d+1); therefore some partition has intersecting hulls. This is a separation-theorem proof of Radon, but it is less elementary and its separation/dimension argument must be stated fully.

existingReferences.label: Matoušek, Lectures on Discrete Geometry
existingReferences.locator: Chapter 1, Radon theorem

tasks.entryDescription: Affine dependence and sign partition; convex-hull separation; linear-algebra nullspace argument.
tasks.currentSketch: Form the (d+1)×(d+2) matrix whose columns are (x_i,1). Its nullspace contains a nonzero vector a. The last row gives Σa_i=0 and the first d rows Σa_ix_i=0; splitting the signs of a and normalizing yields equal convex combinations from disjoint point subsets.

tasks.entryDescription: Augmenting paths/residual graph; linear-programming duality; circulation/polyhedral integrality.
tasks.currentSketch: Run augmenting paths until none remains. Let S be vertices reachable from source in residual graph. Every edge S→Sᶜ is saturated and every edge Sᶜ→S carries zero flow, so flow value equals cut capacity. Weak duality bounds any flow by every cut, proving optimality; integer capacities give an integral max flow.

existingReferences.label: Ahuja, Magnanti & Orlin, Network Flows

tasks.entryDescription: Laplacian cofactor and determinant expansion; electrical-network spanning-tree identity; all-minors/forest counting.
tasks.currentSketch: Delete one row and column of the graph Laplacian L. By Cauchy–Binet, det(L̂) sums squared determinants of incidence submatrices indexed by edge sets of size n−1. Such determinant is ±1 exactly for a spanning tree and 0 otherwise, so the cofactor counts spanning trees.

tasks.entryDescription: Finite-subset compactness/König lemma for countable locally finite cases; maximal matching and augmenting paths; choice/Zorn argument under stated cardinal assumptions.
tasks.routeTitle: Finite-subset compactness/König lemma for countable locally finite cases
tasks.currentSketch: Finite Hall: choose a maximum matching. If an unmatched left vertex exists, follow alternating paths; Hall’s condition prevents the reached left set from having fewer neighboring right vertices, so an augmenting path must exist, contradiction. Infinite variants need conditions: compactness/König handles countable locally finite graphs; arbitrary sets generally require stronger cardinal Hall conditions and choice.

existingReferences.label: Diestel, Graph Theory
existingReferences.locator: Matching chapter; infinite Hall theorem depends on exact neighborhood/cardinality hypotheses

tasks.entryName: Kruskal's theorem (finite graphs have finite obstruction sets under the minor relation)
tasks.entryDescription: Minimal-bad-sequence proof; tree embedding/wqo argument; algebraic proof via graph-minor structure (advanced).
tasks.currentSketch: Assume a bad sequence of finite trees, and choose lexicographically a minimal bad sequence (each term has minimal size among choices that can extend the prefix). Replace infinitely many terms by their proper rooted subtrees; the subsequence of roots’ child forests is well-quasi-ordered by induction/product closure, yielding an earlier tree embedding into a later one, contradiction. Graph-minor theorem is much deeper; tree wqo alone is not its proof.

existingReferences.label: Robertson & Seymour, Graph Minors XX: Wagner’s conjecture
existingReferences.locator: Peer-reviewed proof of graph minor well-quasi-ordering; minimal bad sequence argument

tasks.entryDescription: Homology/degree; local homology and orientation; contradiction using compactness and boundary/sphere separation.
tasks.currentSketch: Assume a continuous injection f:U⊂R^n→R^n has image not open at f(x). Local homology at x is H_n(U,U\{x})≅Z, while at a boundary point of f(U) the corresponding local homology in the target complement vanishes; the homeomorphism U≅f(U) induced by injectivity contradicts this. This uses local compactness/degree or homology machinery.

existingReferences.label: Hatcher, Algebraic Topology
existingReferences.locator: Chapter 2, homology and degree methods for invariance of domain
